{{technical|date=June 2017}}

The '''unique homomorphic extension theorem''' is a result in [[mathematical logic]] which formalizes the intuition that the truth or falsity of a statement can be deduced from the truth values of its parts.<ref>Gallier (2003), p. 25</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/springer_10.1007-3-540-45402-0|page=[https://archive.org/details/springer_10.1007-3-540-45402-0/page/n396 383]|title=Logic Programming and Nonmonotonic Reasoning: 6th International Conference, LPNMR 2001, Vienna, Austria, September 17-19, 2001. Proceedings|last=Eiter|first=Thomas|last2=Faber|first2=Wolfgang|last3=Trusczynksi|first3=Miroslaw|date=2003-08-06|publisher=Springer|isbn=9783540454021|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PugACAAAQBAJ&pg=PA65|title=Fuzzy Logic and Applications: 6th International Workshop, WILF 2005, Crema, Italy, September 15-17, 2005, Revised Selected Papers|last=Bloch|first=Isabelle|author1-link=Isabelle Bloch|last2=Petrosino|first2=Alfredo|last3=Tettamanzi|first3=Andrea G. B.|date=2006-02-15|publisher=Springer|isbn=9783540325307|language=en}}</ref>

== The lemma ==
Let '''A''' be a non-empty set, '''X''' a subset of '''A''', '''F''' a set of functions in '''A''', and <math> X_+ </math> the inductive closure of '''X''' under '''F'''.

Let be '''B''' any non-empty set and let '''G''' be the set of functions on '''B''', such that there is a function <math>d:F\to G</math> in '''G''' that maps with each function '''''f''''' of arity '''''n''''' in '''F''' the following function <math>d(f):B^n\to B</math> in '''G''' (G cannot be a [[bijection]]).

From this lemma we can now build the concept of unique homomorphic extension.

== The theorem ==
If <math> X_+ </math> is a free set generated by '''X''' and '''F''', for each function <math>h:X\to B</math> there is a single function <math>\hat h:X_+\to B</math> such that:

: <math>\forall x\in X, \hat h(x)= h(x); \qquad (1)</math>

For each function ''f'' of arity ''n'' > 0, for each <math>x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X^n_+,</math>

: <math>\hat h(f(x_1, \ldots, x_n)) = g(\hat h(x_1),\ldots,\hat h(x_n)), \text{ where } g=d(f) \qquad (2)</math>
[[File:ConjuntosExtendidos.png|center|340x340px]]
[[File:FuncoesdeExtensao.png|center|320x320px]]

== Consequence ==
The identities seen in (1) e (2) show that <math>\hat h</math> is an homomorphism, specifically named the ''unique homomorphic extension'' of <math>h</math>. To prove the theorem, two requirements must be met: to prove that the extension (<math>\hat h</math>) exists and is unique (assuring the lack of bijections).

=== Proof of the theorem ===
We must define a sequence of functions <math> h_i:X_i\to B </math> inductively, satisfying conditions (1) and (2) restricted to <math>X_i</math>. For this, we define <math>h_0=h</math>, and given <math>h_i</math> then <math>h_{i+1}</math>shall have the following graph:

: <math>{\{(f(x_1,\ldots,x_n),g(h_i(x_1),\ldots,h_i(x_n))) \mid (x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in X^n_i - X^n_{i-1},f\in F\}} \cup {\operatorname{graph}(h_i)} \text{ with } g=d(f)</math>

First we must be certain the graph actually has functionality, since <math>X_+</math> is a free set, from the lemma we have  <math>f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in X_{i+1} - X_i</math> when <math>(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in X^n_i - X^n_{i-1},(i\geq 0)</math>, so we only have to determine the functionality for the left side of the union. Knowing that the elements of '''G''' are functions(again, as defined by the lemma), the only instance where <math>(x,y)\in graph(h_i)</math> and <math>(x,z)\in graph(h_i)</math> for some <math>x\in X_{i+1} - X_i</math> is possible is if we have  <math> x=f(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=f'(y_1,\ldots,y_n) </math>  for some <math>(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in X^m_i - X^m_{i-1},(y_1,\ldots,y_n)\in X^n_i - X^n_{i-1}</math> and for some generators <math>f</math> and <math>{f'}</math> in <math>F</math>.

Since <math> f(X^m_+) </math> and <math> {f'}(X^n_+) </math>  are disjoint when <math>f\neq {f'},f(x_1,\ldots,x_m) = f'(y_1,\ldots,Y_n)</math> this implies <math>f=f' </math> and <math> m=n</math>. Being all <math>f\in F </math> in <math> X^n_+</math>, we must have <math>x_j=y_j,\forall j,1\leq j\leq n</math>.

Then we have <math>y=z=g(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> with <math> g=d(f) </math>, displaying functionality.

Before moving further we must make use of a new lemma that determines the rules for partial functions, it may be written as:
  (3)Be <math>(f_n)_{n\geq 0}</math> a sequence of partial functions <math>f_n:A\to B</math> such that <math>f_n\subseteq f_{n+1},\forall n\geq 0</math>. Then, <math>g=(A,\bigcup graph(f_n),B)</math> is a [[partial function]]. [http://phil.gu.se/logic/books/Gallier:Logic_For_Computer_Science.pdf] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170712195613/http://phil.gu.se/logic/books/Gallier:Logic_For_Computer_Science.pdf |date=2017-07-12 }}
Using (3), <math>\hat h =\bigcup_{i\geq 0} h_i</math> is a partial function. Since  <math> dom(\hat h)=\bigcup dom(h_i)=\bigcup X_i=X_+</math> then <math>\hat h</math> is total in <math>X_+</math>.

Furthermore, it is clear from the definition of <math>h_i</math> that <math>\hat h</math> satisfies (1) and (2). To prove the uniqueness of <math>\hat h</math>, or any other function <math>{h'}</math> that satisfies (1) and (2), it is enough to use a simple induction that shows <math>\hat h</math> and <math>{h'}</math> work for <math>X_i,\forall i\geq 0</math>, and such is proved the Theorem of the Unique Homomorphic Extension.[http://phil.gu.se/logic/books/Gallier:Logic_For_Computer_Science.pdf] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170712195613/http://phil.gu.se/logic/books/Gallier:Logic_For_Computer_Science.pdf |date=2017-07-12 }}

== Example of a particular case ==
We can use the theorem of unique homomorphic extension for calculating numeric expressions over whole numbers. First, we must define the following:

: <math> A=\Sigma^*</math> where <math>\Sigma= \mathrm{Variables} \cup \{0,1,2,\ldots,9\} \cup \{+,-,*\} \cup \{(,)\}, \text{ where }| *=\mathrm{Variables} \cup \{{0,\ldots,9}\}</math>

Be <math>F =\{{f-,f+,f*}\}</math>

<math>f:\Sigma^*\to \Sigma^*_{w\mapsto {-w}} </math>

<math>f:\Sigma^*x\Sigma^*\to \Sigma^*_{w_1,w_2\mapsto {w_1+w_2}} </math>

<math>f:\Sigma^*x\Sigma^*\to \Sigma^*_{w_1,w_2\mapsto {w_1*w_2}} </math>

Be <math>EXPR</math> he inductive closure of <math>X</math> under <math>F</math> and be<math>B=\Z, G={\{Soma(-.-),Mult(-,-),Menos(-)}\}</math>

Be <math>d:F\to G</math>

<math>d({f-})=menos</math>

<math>d({f+})=mais</math>

<math>d({f*})=mult</math>

Then <math>\hat h:X_+\to\{{0,1}\}</math> will be a function that calculates recursively the truth-value of a proposition, and in a way, will be an extension of the function <math>h:X\to\{{0,1}\}</math>that associates a truth-value to each atomic proposition, such that:

(1)<math>\hat h (\phi) = h(\phi)</math>

(2)<math>\hat h({(\neg\phi)})=NAO(\hat h(\psi))</math> (Negation)

<math>\hat h({(\rho\land \theta)})= E(\hat h(\rho),\hat h(\theta))</math> (AND Operator)

<math>\hat h({(\rho\lor \theta)})= OU(\hat h(\rho),\hat h(\theta))</math> (OR Operator)

<math>\hat h({(\rho\to \theta)})= SE\,ENTAO(\hat h(\rho),\hat h(\theta))</math> (IF-THEN Operator)
